The body of Deputy Marshal Vincent Bustamante was found Wednesday in Juarez, Mexico. The body of Deputy Marshal Vincent Bustamante -- who faced federal charges of stealing weapons and other government property -- was found in Juarez on Wednesday, said Marshals Service spokesman Jeff Carter. Bustamante appeared to have been shot in the back of the head, a federal law enforcement source said. Chihuahua state police said the body had multiple wounds to the head -- apparently consistent with an execution-style shooting, according to Edgar Roman, a reporter with XHIJ television in Juarez.  Watch where the U.S. Marshal's body was found » . Bustamante, 48, was charged with stealing U.S. government property including Glock and Ruger handguns, a shotgun and a pair of binoculars, according to court documents. According to the federal source, who was not authorized to speak about details of the case and asked not to be named, a pawnshop owner became suspicious when Bustamante attempted to pawn a shotgun and called the U.S. Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives. The source said Bustamante would buy back items he had pawned on his pay days and return them. Bustamante's attorney, Mike Torres, said a warrant was issued for Bustamante's arrest after he failed to appear at a court hearing last week. He said Bustamante was a 17-year veteran of the marshals and a former El Paso Police officer who lived in El Paso with his wife and two children. "He was a familiar face around the federal courthouse here," Torres said. "I'm very shocked by this and very saddened. "He had a lot of friends and a lot of people that cared about him." Carter said Bustamante was on administrative leave from the marshals and had been required to turn in his gun and badge. He said Bustamante had not been in Mexico on marshals business and that all of the weapons he was charged with stealing had been recovered. Carter said Bustamante was on "modified status" with the marshals, meaning he had been required to turn in his gun and badge outside of his official work hours. "What I can tell you is that the U.S. Marshals Service is saddened by the death of Deputy Bustamante and our thoughts and prayers are with his family," he said. Carter said U.S. marshals are working with the FBI and Mexican authorities to investigate the death. He said an autopsy will be conducted in Mexico, and another may be conducted once Bustamante's body is returned to the United States. Juarez, which sits across the border from El Paso, Texas, has become one of the major battlegrounds as drug cartels fight both each other and Mexican authorities. The conflict has made violence increasingly common in Juarez, Tijuana and other Mexican border towns. More than 400 deaths in the region have been attributed to the fighting this year. CNN's Anderson Cooper, Emily Robards and Devon Sayers contributed to this report.

For decades, Ciudad Juarez has occupied a singular place in the global imagination. Perched along the dusty banks of the Rio Grande, directly across from El Paso, Texas, the Mexican border city has long been a focal point for international trade, migration, and complex socio-political dynamics. When major media outlets like CNN send correspondents to the region, the camera lenses often capture a city defined by stark contrasts and profound resilience.

To many international viewers, their first introduction to Juarez came through breaking news broadcasts. During the height of the border conflicts and cartel rivalries in the late 2000s and early 2010s, CNN crews were a frequent presence on Avenida Juárez and near the international bridges. Their reports chronicled the harsh realities of a city under siege, transmitting images of police barricades and desert landscapes to living rooms across the globe.

However, the story of Juarez is far deeper than the tragic headlines that once dominated the evening news. Over the years, coverage has shifted to capture the evolving identity of the metropolis. CNN features have increasingly highlighted the industrial engine of Juarez—its massive network of *maquiladoras* that supply electronics, auto parts, and medical goods to the entire Western Hemisphere. Other reports have showcased the vibrant cultural movements taking root in the city, from grassroots art collectives revitalizing urban spaces to local chefs redefining border cuisine.

Reporting from Juarez requires navigating a tapestry of human experience. Every day, thousands of workers, students, and families cross the Paso del Norte Bridge, embodying an interconnected cross-border reality that defies simple political narratives. For journalists on assignment for CNN, capturing this daily rhythm is essential to telling a complete story. It is a place where economic hardship and immense hope exist side by side, and where the local community continuously works to reshape its future.

Ultimately, Juarez serves as a microcosm for the broader issues facing the modern world: globalization, immigration, and urban endurance. While the city's past challenges remain a part of its history, the ongoing coverage from networks like CNN reminds the world that behind every headline is a dynamic, living city striving to build a legacy of strength and renewal.

"He swore an oath to protect the public and enforce the law. Instead, he sold out his colleagues to the very criminal enterprise he was tasked with dismantling."

### A fatal end to a wild search

Vance’s disappearance in late July prompted an international manhunt led by the FBI and the USMS Office of Professional Responsibility. Authorities believed he had crossed the southern border using a fraudulent passport shortly after learning he was the subject of a federal wiretap.

While Mexican authorities have not formally named suspects in the killing, a U.S. law enforcement source told CNN that investigators suspect Vance was executed by the same cartel he allegedly assisted. 

"When a corrupt insider becomes a high-profile fugitive, they cease to be an asset to these organizations and become a massive liability," the source said. "Once his usefulness vanished and the heat turned up, his protection disappeared."

In a statement to CNN, U.S. Marshals Service Director Ronald L. Davis expressed condolences to Vance’s family while emphasizing the agency's commitment to integrity.

"The allegations against Mr. Vance do not reflect the honorable work performed daily by the men and women of the United States Marshals Service," Davis said. "While this is a tragic end to a deeply troubling chapter, our agency remains committed to transparency and accountability."

Mexican forensic teams are currently performing an autopsy, and the FBI has dispatched a team of agents to Guadalajara to assist in the homicide investigation.
